summary: Fluorometholone acetate 0.1% (FLAREX) is a topical ophthalmic corticosteroid suspension for steroid-responsive inflammatory conditions of the conjunctiva, cornea, and anterior segment of the eye. It is dosed 1-2 drops four times daily after shaking well. Prolonged use can raise intraocular pressure and cause glaucoma, cataract, optic nerve damage, and secondary ocular infection, and it is contraindicated in most ocular viral, fungal, and mycobacterial infections.
indications: Steroid-responsive inflammatory conditions of the palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva
Steroid-responsive inflammatory conditions of the cornea and anterior segment of the eye

dosage.d: 1-2 drops into the conjunctival sac(s) four times daily
dosage.n: Do not discontinue prematurely; reassess if no improvement after 2 weeks
Taper to four times daily thereafter

admin: Instill 1-2 drops into the conjunctival sac(s) four times daily
Do not touch the dropper tip to any surface to avoid contamination
Remove contact lenses before instillation; reinsert 15 minutes after (benzalkonium chloride may be absorbed by soft lenses)
Do not refill the prescription without further evaluation; reassess if no improvement after 2 weeks
moa: Corticosteroids suppress the inflammatory response to mechanical, chemical, or immunologic agents in the eye. The precise mechanism is not fully established, but topical fluorometholone reduces ocular inflammation; it can also raise intraocular pressure in susceptible individuals.

absolute: Acute superficial herpes simplex keratitis, vaccinia, varicella, and most other viral diseases of the cornea and conjunctiva
Acute purulent untreated infections of the eye
Known hypersensitivity to any component of the preparation
relative: Treatment of herpes simplex infection (requires great caution)
Diseases causing thinning of the cornea or sclera (risk of perforation)
monitor: Intraocular pressure if used 10 days or longer
Signs of secondary ocular infection (bacterial, fungal, viral)

preg: Fluorometholone has been embryocidal and teratogenic in rabbits at low multiples of the human ocular dose, producing dose-related fetal loss and abnormalities (cleft palate, deformed rib cage, anomalous limbs, neural defects such as encephalocele and spina bifida). There are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women; use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: Systemically administered corticosteroids appear in human milk and could suppress growth or interfere with endogenous corticosteroid production. It is not known whether topical ophthalmic use produces detectable amounts in milk; exercise caution when administered to a nursing woman.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is provided; systemic absorption from topical ophthalmic use is minimal.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is provided; systemic absorption from topical ophthalmic use is minimal.

interactions.diagnostics: Monitor intraocular pressure (tonometry) with use of 10 days or longer

serious: Elevated intraocular pressure / glaucoma with optic nerve damage
Visual acuity and visual field defects
Secondary ocular infection from suppressed host response
Perforation of the globe in corneal/scleral thinning
rare: Cushing's syndrome and adrenal suppression after very frequent use (especially in very young children)
emergency: Acute rise in intraocular pressure with vision loss

monitoring: Intraocular pressure (tonometry) if used for 10 days or longer
Signs of secondary bacterial, fungal, or viral infection
Corneal and scleral integrity (slit-lamp, fluorescein staining where appropriate)
Visual acuity and clinical response (re-evaluate if no improvement in 2 weeks)
counsel: Shake well before use and do not touch the dropper tip to any surface

Remove contact lenses before instilling and reinsert 15 minutes later
Do not stop therapy prematurely and do not refill without re-evaluation
Report eye pain, worsening redness, vision changes, or discharge promptly
pk: Local anti-inflammatory effect after topical instillation
Acts locally at ocular tissues; minimal systemic absorption
Not characterized for topical ophthalmic use (minimal systemic levels)
Dosed four times daily to maintain effect
Store upright at 2-25 C; protect from freezing
pearls: Contraindicated in herpes simplex keratitis and most ocular viral, fungal, and mycobacterial infections
Monitor intraocular pressure if used 10 days or longer - steroids can cause glaucoma and cataract
Shake well before each use (it is a suspension)
Fluorometholone tends to raise IOP more slowly than dexamethasone, but the eventual rise can be comparable
Prescribe no more than one bottle initially and do not refill without re-evaluation
missed: Instill the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule; do not double the dose.
overdose: Topical ophthalmic overdose is unlikely to cause acute systemic toxicity. Excessive or prolonged use can cause elevated intraocular pressure, glaucoma, cataract, and increased risk of secondary infection. If accidentally ingested, treat symptomatically. Flush the eye with water if overapplied and contact a clinician if irritation persists.
